Practical No. 1

                                         Study of Hemichordates

Learning outcomes: Students will be able to classify hemichordates and recognize their
habitat, diversity of food, adaptation for protection and reproduction on this earth.

         Hemichordates are marine animals. These animals are also called as Acorn Worms. They were initially
grouped under Phylum Chordata. But, research has proven that none of these organisms does not have a post-
anal tail or even the notochord, which is a distinguishing feature of chordates. Hence, these animals have been
given a separate phylum, called the Hemichordata.

       They are mostly burrowers in sand or mud, or live in algae or beneath stones. Their long bodies are
divided into an anterior proboscis, a short collar and a long trunk. They vary greatly in size, ranging from a few
millimetres to almost one and a half meters. Balanoglossus a hemichordate species can be of 1.5 meters in length.
These species feed on small organic particles. They can be either filter feeders or substrate eaters.

Classification of Phylum Hemichordata
Phylum Hemichordata is again divided into two classes:

•   Enteropneusta: This class includes acorn worms. They have a vermiform body and are found on sandy
    beaches near seas in warm climates.

•   Pterobranchia: They have a tube-dwelling and live in deep sea waters. They are bottom dwellers who
    attach to other organisms for their survival.

Acorn worms are solitary, wormlike, bilaterally symmetrical animals, often brilliantly coloured. They are
known as acorn worms because of the appearance of the proboscis and collar.

Characteristic Features of Acorn worm

       Proboscis is short, conical projection at the worm’s anterior end .A ring like collar is posterior to
proboscis and an elongated trunk is third division of the body.
        Mouth is located ventrally between proboscis and collar, A variable number of pharyngeal slits are
positioned laterally on the trunk.
        There is no central nervous system: nerve tissue is concentrated in the collar, which is linked with
a nervous system in the epidermis, or outer covering. The circulatory system usually includes a contractile
heart like vesicle, blood vessels, and sinuses. The pharynx may be perforated by numerous paired gill slits,
or they may be absent.
        Acorn worms are suspension feeders, capturing minute animals as they drift by in the water organisms
on their proboscis. Many hemichordates have a larval stage in their life cycle; the larvae, called tornariae,
swim using microscopic hairs called cilia.

      Sexes are separate or united. Reproduction is mostly sexual reproduction. Fertilization is external.
Development is mostly indirect. But a few species exhibit direct development.

       The hemichordates have evolutionary links with both chordates and echinoderms (e.g., starfish, sea
urchins); however, precise relationships are still being actively studied.

                                         Study of Urochordates
Learning outcome: Students will understand the classification of urochordates and will
learn their habitat, food availability, adaptation for protection and reproduction.

        Urochordata come under the classification of Cephalochordates. They are a subphylum of the
Phylum Chordates and consist only of marine filter-feeding invertebrates that are found in seawater. They
feed on planktonic particles

         The Urochordata, sometimes known as the Tunicates, are commonly known as "sea squirts." The body
of an adult tunicate is quite simple, being essentially a sack with two siphons through which water enters and
exits. Water is filtered inside the sack-shaped body. However, many tunicates have a larva that is free-
swimming and exhibits all chordate characteristics: it has a notochord, a dorsal nerve cord, pharyngeal slits,
and a post-anal tail. This "tadpole larva" will swim for some time; it eventually attaches to a hard substrate,
it loses its tail and ability to move, and its nervous system largely disintegrates.

                       Classification of Aseidia

               Order                  Enterogona
               Genus                  Aseidia

Distribution
Tunicates are distributed in ocean waters from the polar regions to the tropics. Free-swimming tunicates are
found throughout the oceans as plankton, while sessile forms grow mainly on solid surfaces such as wharf
piles, ship hulls, rocks, and the shells of various sea creatures.

Question:
    Differentiate between Urochordata and Cephalochordates.

Solution:
    Urochordates (tunicates) and cephalochordates (lancelets) are both chordates, but they
belong to different subphyla with distinct characteristics.

Differences

1. Body Structure
  ● Urochordates: Simple, sac-like body.
  ● Cephalochordates: Elongated, fish-like body.

2. Notochord Presence
  ● Urochordates: Notochord present only in larval stage.
  ● Cephalochordates: Notochord present throughout life.

3. Dorsal Hollow Nerve Cord
  ● Urochordates: Simple nerve cord.
  ● Cephalochordates: Well-developed dorsal hollow nerve cord.

4. Pharyngeal Slits
  ● Both have pharyngeal slits, but urochordates have a more complex structure.

5. Feeding Mechanism
  ● Urochordates: Filter-feeding using pharyngeal slits.
  ● Cephalochordates: Filter-feeding using pharyngeal slits and cilia.

6. Habitat
  ● Urochordates: Marine, often attached to rocks or reefs.
  ● Cephalochordates: Marine, burrowing in sand.

7. Development
  ● Urochordates: Indirect development with a distinct larval stage.
  ● Cephalochordates: More direct development.

8. Body Wall Composition
  ● Urochordates: Body wall contains a tunic (cellulose-like material).
  ● Cephalochordates: Body wall composed of muscle and connective tissue.

9. Circulatory System
  ● Urochordates: Simple, open circulatory system.
  ● Cephalochordates: Closed circulatory system.

10. Segmentation
  ● Urochordates: Segmentation not evident in adults.
  ● Cephalochordates: Segmentation evident in body musculature.

11. Adult Lifestyle
  ● Urochordates: Often sessile.
  ● Cephalochordates: Active swimmers and burrowers.

12. Nervous System Complexity
  ● Urochordates: Simple nervous system.
  ● Cephalochordates: More complex nervous system.

13. Sensory Organs
  ● Urochordates: Limited sensory organs.
  ● Cephalochordates: More developed sensory organs.

14. Musculature
  ● Urochordates: Simple musculature.
  ● Cephalochordates: Well-developed musculature for swimming and burrowing.

15. Tail Presence
  ● Urochordates: Larvae have a tail; adults often do not.
  ● Cephalochordates: Both larvae and adults have a distinct tail.

   These differences reflect the unique characteristics and evolutionary adaptations of urochordates and
cephalochordates.

 Characteristics of Protochordata (Tunicates & Amphioxus)

• The organisms belonging to the Protochordata are generally known as

   the lower chordates.

• They don’t form a “proper” taxonomic group and are only classified as

   such for convenience purposes.

• However, they do form a major division of Chordata.

• They are also known as Acraniata because they lack a true skull.

Characteristics of Protochordata

• They are generally found in marine water.

• Their body is bilaterally symmetrical, triploblastic, and coelomated.

• At a certain stage of their lives, their body develops a long, rod-like

   structure for support called notochord.

• They exhibit organ system level of organization.

• Eg., Herdmania, Amphioxus.

            Lesson 2
Phylum Hemichordata

Hemichordata (Tunicates & Amphioxus)

• Marine, Solitarily

• Deuterostomate animals with a body divided into three regions: proboscis, collar,

   and trunk; coelom divided into three cavities

• Body is divided into proboscis, collar, and trunk.

• Bilaterally symmetrical

• Primitive notochord restricted to proboscis only, thus called stomochord.

• Triploblastic

• True coelom present

• Straight or U shaped gut with anus

• Nervous system normally diffuse and variable

• Open circulatory system

• Blood has no color and corpuscles.

• Excretory organ- Glomerulus

• Filter feeding

• Four classes- Enteropneusta, Pterobranchia, Planctosphaeroidea, Graptolita

• Eg., Cephalodiscus, Rhabdopeura

            Lesson 3
Class Enteropneusta

Class I – Enteropneusta (Acorn worms)

General Characters
• Marine worms
• Usually range in size between 10 and 40 cm

• More than 70 species

• most occupy U-shaped burrows in sandy

  and muddy substrates between the limits of high and low tides.

Proboscis is a short, conical projection at the worm’s

anterior end.

A ring like collar is posterior to the proboscis

An elongate trunk is the third division of the body

A ciliated epidermis and gland cells cover acorn worms.

The mouth is located ventrally between the proboscis and

the collar.

• A variable number of pharyngeal slits, from a few to several hundred, are

   positioned laterally on the trunk.

• Pharyngeal slits are openings between the anterior region of the digestive

   tract, called the pharynx, and the outside of the body.

                              Lesson 4
Enteropneusta : Feeding, Digestion and
                      Nervous system

Enteropneusta : Feeding

• Cilia and mucus assist acorn worms in feeding.

• Detritus and other particles adhere to the mucus-covered

   proboscis. Tracts of cilia transport food and mucus

   posteriorly and ventrally.

• Ciliary tracts converge near the mouth and form a mucoid string that enters

   the mouth.

• Acorn worms may reject some substances trapped in the mucoid string by

   pulling the proboscis against the collar.

• Ciliary tracts of the collar and trunk transport rejected material and discard it

   posteriorly.

Enteropneusta : Digestion

The digestive tract of enteropneusts is a simple tube.

Food is digested as diverticula of the gut, called hepatic sacs, release enzymes.

The worm extends its posterior end out of the burrow during defecation. At

low tide, coils of fecal material, called castings, lie on the substrate at burrow

openings.

Enteropneusta : Nervous system

The nervous system of enteropneusts is ectodermal in origin

Lies at the base of the ciliated epidermis.

Consists of dorsal and ventral nerve tracts

and a network of epidermal nerve cells, called a nerve plexus.

There are no major ganglia.

Sensory receptors are unspecialized and widely distributed over the body.

                                Lesson 5
Enteropneusta : Respiration, Circulation
                          and Excretion

   Enteropneusta : Respiration
• Because acorn worms are small, respiratory gases and metabolic waste

   products (principally ammonia) probably are exchanged by diffusion across the

   body wall.

• In addition, respiratory gases are exchanged at the pharyngeal slits.

• Cilia associated with pharyngeal slits circulate water into the mouth and out of

   the body through the pharyngeal slits.

• As water passes through the pharyngeal slits, gases are exchanged by diffusion

   between water and blood sinuses surrounding the pharynx.

Enteropneusta : Circulation

The circulatory system of acorn worms consists of one dorsal and one ventral

contractile vessel.

Blood moves anteriorly in the dorsal vessel and posteriorly in the ventral

vessel.

Branches from these vessels lead to open sinuses.

All blood flowing anteriorly passes into a series of blood sinuses, called the

glomerulus, at the base of the proboscis.

   Enteropneusta : Excretion

• Excretory wastes may be filtered through the glomerulus, into the coelom of the

   proboscis,

• Later on release to the outside through one or two pores in the wall of the

   proboscis.

Ciona intestinalis: A Study of Its Classification, Life Cycle,
and Ecological Significance

1. Introduction

Ciona intestinalis, commonly called the sea squirt, is a marine invertebrate belonging to the
subphylum Urochordata (Tunicata). Despite their sedentary adult life, these animals possess key
chordate features such as a notochord and dorsal nerve cord during their larval stage. This unique
combination makes Ciona intestinalis a valuable model for understanding early chordate
evolution and marine ecosystem functioning.

2. Taxonomic Classification

2.1 Scientific Classification

(16)

   •   Kingdom: Animalia
   •   Phylum: Chordata
   •   Subphylum: Urochordata
   •   Class: Ascidiacea
   •   Order: Phlebobranchia
   •   Family: Cionidae
   •   Genus: Ciona
   •   Species: Ciona intestinalis

3. Morphology and Anatomy

3.1 External Features

Ciona intestinalis has a soft, cylindrical, translucent body covered by a cellulose-like tunic called
tunicin. It attaches to hard surfaces like rocks or ship hulls via its base. The body includes an oral
siphon for water intake and an atrial siphon for expelling filtered water.

3.2 Internal Structure

Inside, it contains a large pharyngeal basket with numerous gill slits for filter feeding. Although
the adult lacks a notochord and dorsal nerve cord, these are well developed in the larval stage.
The adult has a simple nervous system and an open circulatory system.

4. Life Cycle

4.1 Reproduction and Fertilization

Ciona intestinalis is hermaphroditic and reproduces via external fertilization. Eggs and sperm are
released into the water through the atrial siphon. Once fertilized, embryos develop rapidly.

4.2 Larval Stage

The embryo develops into a free-swimming tadpole larva that possesses all key chordate
features— a notochord, dorsal nerve cord, tail, and a brain-like structure. This stage lasts only a
few hours to promote dispersal.

4.3 Metamorphosis and Adult Stage

After swimming, the larva settles on a substrate and undergoes metamorphosis. It absorbs its tail
and notochord, reconfigures its body structure, and becomes a sessile adult that remains attached
to the surface.

5. Ecological Significance

5.1 Water Filtration and Nutrient Cycling

As a filter feeder, Ciona intestinalis removes plankton and organic particles from seawater,
contributing to water purification and nutrient cycling. One individual can filter several liters of
water per hour.

5.2 Role in Marine Habitats

Aggregations of Ciona intestinalis form microhabitats for microorganisms and juvenile marine
animals. This enhances biodiversity and stabilizes benthic ecosystems in coastal environments.

5.3 Invasive Potential and Biofouling

Introduced globally via ship ballast water, Ciona intestinalis often becomes invasive. It can
outcompete native species and cause biofouling problems on marine infrastructure and
aquaculture farms.

6. Scientific and Human Relevance

6.1 Model Organism in Research

The genome of Ciona intestinalis is compact and fully sequenced, making it ideal for
developmental and genetic studies. It provides insight into vertebrate evolution, particularly the
origin of the notochord and nervous system.

6.2 Biomedical and Industrial Applications

Compounds derived from its tunic have shown antimicrobial and antifouling properties. These
bioactive substances are being studied for pharmaceutical and marine engineering applications.

7. Conclusion

Ciona intestinalis is a key species linking invertebrates and vertebrates through its evolutionary
traits. Its biphasic lifecycle, efficient filtration, and adaptability give it both ecological
importance and scientific value. While beneficial in research and ecosystems, its invasive
behavior requires careful monitoring in non-native habitats.

Explain the major classes included within the Subphylum Craniata and
Provide examples of each.

The Subphylum Craniata (sometimes used interchangeably with Vertebrata) comprises those
chordates that possess a true skull (cranium) enclosing the brain. Below is an overview of its
major (extant) classes, arranged phylogenetically from the most “primitive” jawless groups up
through the jawed vertebrates.

1. Class Myxini (Hagfishes)

   •   Key features:
          o Jawless, eel-like body
          o Movable knotting behavior for feeding
          o Produces large quantities of slime as a defense
   •   Example:
          o Eptatretus stoutii (Pacific hagfish)

2. Class Petromyzontida (Lampreys)

   •   Key features:
          o Also jawless but with a toothed, suction-cup mouth
          o Lifecycle often includes a filter-feeding larval (ammocoete) stage
          o Many are parasitic as adults
   •   Example:
          o Petromyzon marinus (sea lamprey)

Gnathostomata (Jawed Vertebrates)

With the evolution of jaws, vertebrates diversify into bony and cartilaginous groups.

3. Class Chondrichthyes (Cartilaginous Fishes)

   •   Key features:
          o Skeleton made of cartilage rather than bone
          o Placoid scales (“dermal denticles”)
          o Includes both constantly-moving filter feeders and active predators

Reptiles have a relatively efficient respiratory system adapted to their needs:

1. **Lungs**: Reptiles have well-developed lungs with a higher surface area for gas exchange
compared to amphibians. Some reptiles, like crocodiles, have a diaphragm-like muscle to assist
in breathing.

2. **Ventilation Mechanisms**: Many reptiles use a combination of muscular contractions and
changes in body cavity pressure to move air in and out of the lungs.

3. **Efficiency**: Reptiles generally have a slower metabolism and can efficiently extract oxygen
from the air they breathe, which suits their often lower activity levels compared to birds and
mammals.

### Skull Modification in Kinetic Skull

The kinetic skull in reptiles features:

1. **Mobile Joints**: Unlike in mammals, reptilian skulls have flexible joints, particularly in the
jaws and between skull bones. This allows for a wide gape and effective capture and
manipulation of prey.

2. **Quadrate Bone Mobility**: In many reptiles, the quadrate bone (part of the jaw) can move,
contributing to the flexibility of the jaw.

3. **Benefits**: This skull structure is advantageous for feeding, allowing reptiles to consume
prey larger than their head or to move their jaws in a more varied manner.

### Osmoregulation and Its Importance

**Osmoregulation** is the process by which organisms maintain the balance of water and salts
in their bodies. This is crucial for several reasons:

1. **Homeostasis**: It helps maintain internal fluid balance, which is essential for proper
cellular function and overall homeostasis.

2. **Environmental Adaptation**: In aquatic environments, especially in saltwater, organisms
must expel excess salts and retain water. In freshwater environments, they need to excrete
excess water and retain salts.

3. **Species-Specific Strategies**:

  - **Fish**: Marine fish excrete excess salts through specialized cells in their gills and
concentrate their urine. Freshwater fish, on the other hand, excrete dilute urine and actively
absorb salts through their gills.

  - **Other Animals**: Terrestrial animals have adaptations to conserve water, such as kidneys
that produce concentrated urine.

### Bony Fishes and Their Environmental Significance

There are approximately **32,000 species** of bony fishes, making them the largest group of
vertebrates. Their environmental significance includes:

1. **Ecological Roles**: Bony fishes occupy various ecological niches as predators, prey, and
competitors. They play key roles in food webs and ecosystems.

2. **Coral Reef Health**: Many bony fish species are vital to the health of coral reefs, providing
essential ecological services such as algae control and reef structure maintenance.

3. **Nutrient Cycling**: They contribute to nutrient cycling in aquatic environments by
participating in the breakdown of organic matter and cycling nutrients through the food web.

4. **Economic Importance**: Bony fishes are crucial for commercial and recreational fisheries,
contributing to human economies and food sources.

Phylum Hemichordata

Hemichordata (Tunicates & Amphioxus)

• Marine, Solitarily

• Deuterostomate animals with a body divided into three regions: proboscis, collar,

   and trunk; coelom divided into three cavities

• Body is divided into proboscis, collar, and trunk.

• Bilaterally symmetrical

            Lesson 3
Class Enteropneusta

Class I – Enteropneusta (Acorn worms)

General Characters
• Marine worms
• Usually range in size between 10 and 40 cm

• More than 70 species

• most occupy U-shaped burrows in sandy

  and muddy substrates between the limits of high and low tides.

Proboscis is a short, conical projection at the worm’s

anterior end.

A ring like collar is posterior to the proboscis

An elongate trunk is the third division of the body

A ciliated epidermis and gland cells cover acorn worms.

The mouth is located ventrally between the proboscis and

the collar.

• A variable number of pharyngeal slits, from a few to several hundred, are

   positioned laterally on the trunk.

• Pharyngeal slits are openings between the anterior region of the digestive

   tract, called the pharynx, and the outside of the body.

                              Lesson 4
Enteropneusta : Feeding, Digestion and
                      Nervous system

Enteropneusta : Feeding

• Cilia and mucus assist acorn worms in feeding.

• Detritus and other particles adhere to the mucus-covered

   proboscis. Tracts of cilia transport food and mucus

   posteriorly and ventrally.

• Ciliary tracts converge near the mouth and form a mucoid string that enters

   the mouth.

• Acorn worms may reject some substances trapped in the mucoid string by

   pulling the proboscis against the collar.

• Ciliary tracts of the collar and trunk transport rejected material and discard it

   posteriorly.

Enteropneusta : Digestion

The digestive tract of enteropneusts is a simple tube.

Food is digested as diverticula of the gut, called hepatic sacs, release enzymes.

The worm extends its posterior end out of the burrow during defecation. At

low tide, coils of fecal material, called castings, lie on the substrate at burrow

openings.

Enteropneusta : Nervous system

The nervous system of enteropneusts is ectodermal in origin

Lies at the base of the ciliated epidermis.

Consists of dorsal and ventral nerve tracts

and a network of epidermal nerve cells, called a nerve plexus.

There are no major ganglia.

Sensory receptors are unspecialized and widely distributed over the body.

                                Lesson 5
Enteropneusta : Respiration, Circulation
                          and Excretion

   Enteropneusta : Respiration
• Because acorn worms are small, respiratory gases and metabolic waste

   products (principally ammonia) probably are exchanged by diffusion across the

   body wall.

• In addition, respiratory gases are exchanged at the pharyngeal slits.

• Cilia associated with pharyngeal slits circulate water into the mouth and out of

   the body through the pharyngeal slits.

• As water passes through the pharyngeal slits, gases are exchanged by diffusion

   between water and blood sinuses surrounding the pharynx.

Enteropneusta : Circulation

The circulatory system of acorn worms consists of one dorsal and one ventral

contractile vessel.

Blood moves anteriorly in the dorsal vessel and posteriorly in the ventral

vessel.

Branches from these vessels lead to open sinuses.

All blood flowing anteriorly passes into a series of blood sinuses, called the

glomerulus, at the base of the proboscis.

   Enteropneusta : Excretion

• Excretory wastes may be filtered through the glomerulus, into the coelom of the

   proboscis,

• Later on release to the outside through one or two pores in the wall of the

   proboscis.
